paper.title: Large Language Models as Tool Makers
paper.central_claim: LATM, a closed-loop framework where a strong LLM (tool maker) creates reusable Python utility functions that a lightweight LLM (tool user) applies, with a dispatcher LLM providing a functional cache, achieves performance equivalent to using GPT-4 for both roles at significantly reduced inference cost (Abstract; Sec 1, 3-5).

evidence.quote: With GPT-4 as the tool maker and GPT-3.5 as the tool user, LATM demonstrates performance equivalent to using GPT-4 for both roles, but with a significantly reduced inference cost.
evidence.support_explanation: Central claim: accuracy parity with GPT-4-for-both-roles plus significantly lower cost.

evidence.quote: In our experiments, we use 3 demonstrations for this stage. If the proposed tool is unexecutable or encounters errors, tool maker appends the error messages to the history and makes another attempt.
evidence.support_explanation: Candidate generation: programming-by-example from 3 demos; execution errors are the feedback signal, appended to history for the next attempt.

evidence.quote: We utilize 3 validation samples in our experiments. If the tool fails any of these tests, the tool maker records the error in its history and makes an attempt to rectify the issues within the unit tests (this procedure will only correct the function calls in the unit test part and will not correct the function).
evidence.support_explanation: Admission gate = unit tests on only 3 validation samples; a test failure triggers repair of the TEST call parsing only, not of the function.

evidence.quote: it provides examples that demonstrate how to convert natural language questions into function calls
evidence.support_explanation: Authors state the verification stage mainly yields NL-question -> function-call demonstrations for the tool user (plus reliability check).

evidence.quote: If the execution or verification fails over a preset threshold, the Tool Making stage is viewed as failed.
evidence.support_explanation: Reject rule: tool-making trial is discarded after exceeding the retry threshold (3 per Sec 5.1).

evidence.quote: The prompt for this stage is the wrapped tool which contains the function for solving the task and demonstrations of how to convert a task query into a function call.
evidence.support_explanation: Persisted artifact (function + use-case demos) is the later-task prompt read by the tool user.

evidence.quote: The dispatcher maintains a repository of existing tools crafted by the tool maker in the format of function APIs.
evidence.support_explanation: Persistence/store: a repository of function APIs consulted by a dispatcher LLM.

evidence.quote: We divide each dataset into training, validation, and test sets, containing 3, 3, and 240 instances, respectively.
evidence.support_explanation: Tool is built from 3 train + 3 validation instances; 240 disjoint test instances per task.

evidence.quote: We set the maximal retry times to be 3 for the tool-proposing and tool-verification stages.
evidence.support_explanation: Retry budget for tool making. (Temperature 0.3 in tool making, 0.0 in tool use, same section.)

evidence.quote: we only observe 2 cases out of the 60 trials that the tool maker can correct its mistakes with the guide of error messages
evidence.support_explanation: Execution/verification feedback rarely repairs a bad tool (2/60), so feedback-driven repair is not load-bearing in this paper.

evidence.quote: with the help of the tool, a lightweight model like GPT-3.5 Turbo can achieve performance on par with GPT-4
evidence.support_explanation: Authors read Table 2 as GPT-3.5 + tool ~ GPT-4.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (rows GPT-3.5 CoT / LATM, GPT-4 CoT / LATM)
evidence.support_explanation: Table 2 values (extracted in row order): GPT-3.5 CoT 66.4/61.6/20.4/59.2/0.0/18.9 vs LATM 79.7/99.6/92.2/98.3/100/100 on LogicalDed(5)/TrackShuffled(5)/Dyck/WordSort/CRT/ScheduleMeeting; GPT-4 CoT 88.8/100/63.6/90.9/0/55.6 vs LATM 86.6/100/87.5/99.1/100/100. LATM GPT-3.5 79.7 vs GPT-4 CoT 88.8 on Logical Deduction is a ~9-pt gap. No uncertainty reported.

evidence.quote: At the time of writing this paper, C is over 15x larger than c.
evidence.support_explanation: Cost column is analytic only: O(nc) for GPT-3.5 CoT, O(nc + C) for LATM-GPT-3.5, O(nC) for GPT-4; C>15c is the only quantitative cost fact; no dollar/token totals.

evidence.quote: The few-shot CoT demonstrations for the first four tasks are provided by Suzgun et al. (2022), while for the last two tasks, we apply direct few-shot prompting without CoT.
evidence.support_explanation: Baselines: few-shot CoT (Suzgun) on 4 tasks; direct few-shot prompting (no CoT, no program-aided baseline) on CRT and Schedule Meeting.

evidence.quote: GPT-4 occasionally superfluously closes some brackets within the argument instead of leaving the argument unchanged
evidence.support_explanation: Failure analysis of the one task where GPT-3.5 as tool user beats GPT-4 (92.2 vs 87.5): the user model pre-solves arguments.

evidence.quote: For hard tasks like Logical Deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects, GPT-3.5 Turbo fails in all trials, showing the necessity of using a more powerful model as tool maker.
evidence.support_explanation: Tool-maker capability ablation (author-reported).

GPT-4 maker valid-tool success per task over 5 trials: LD 3/5, TSO 4/5, Dyck 5/5, WS 5/5, CRT 5/5, Schedule 3/5; GPT-3.5 maker 0/5 on LD, TSO, Schedule. Failed trials are reported, but cost of failed trials is not folded into the cost model.

evidence.quote: the major failure reason is that the tool is not general enough and may only work on the training samples
evidence.support_explanation: Reported failure mode of generated tools: overfit to the demonstrations - a weak admission gate (3 demos + 3 validation).

evidence.quote: Over multiple runs, the accuracy of making the correct decision stands at 96% ± 3%
evidence.support_explanation: Dispatcher decision accuracy (also 95% ± 2% for tool identification over five random test-set constructions, 100 samples each). Only dispatcher classification is measured.

evidence.quote: all while maintaining high performance
evidence.support_explanation: Streaming-setting claim; no end-to-end accuracy/cost for the stream pipeline (dispatcher + maker + user) is reported.

evidence.quote: Of all the models, GPT-3.5 Turbo demonstrates the best trade-off between performance and cost.
evidence.support_explanation: Tool-user capability sweep with the same GPT-4 tool (per-1K-token prices given); only data on cost trade-off.

evidence.quote: We observe that using CoT from a large model has a similar or even worse performance than human-written CoT, which is much worse than LATM.
evidence.support_explanation: Partial control: reusing GPT-4 reasoning text (CoT) as the retained artifact instead of code, on two tasks.
GPT-4 CoT 36.8 (LD) / 63.2 (TSO); human CoT 66.4 / 61.6; LATM 79.7 / 99.6. Only 2 tasks; zero-shot "Let's think step by step" CoT-making.

evidence.quote: An exciting avenue for future research is enabling the tool maker to refine and upgrade existing tools to manage new problem instances
evidence.support_explanation: Authors concede tool refinement/upgrade after deployment is not done: the tool is made once, not updated.

evidence.quote: Concurrent and independent to our work, several early attempts have been made towards using LLMs to make tools.
evidence.support_explanation: Nearest neighbors are treated as concurrent (Voyager, CREATOR).

evidence.quote: However, we also underscore the significance of tool reusability and cost-effectiveness stemming from the division of labor.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors name the differentiators vs concurrent tool-making: reusability and maker/user cost split. No empirical comparison to these neighbors.

evidence.quote: However, their primary focus is on using Python executors to accurately solve sub-steps involving arithmetic reasoning
evidence.support_explanation: Distinction from Chameleon/PAL/PoT: per-instance execution vs reusable tools (next sentence: "we use Python executors to create reusable tools for addressing other task instances"). PAL/PoT-style per-instance code is not run as a baseline.

evidence.quote: However, the applicability of these tool-using methods is largely contingent on the availability of suitable tools.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap 1: tool availability (tools must pre-exist).

evidence.quote: directly utilizing a powerful LLM to solve all the instances can result in high costs
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap 2: serving cost of using the strong model for every instance.

evidence.quote: the availability of A and B are randomly sampled from 8:00-18:00 with 30 minutes as the granularity
evidence.support_explanation: Schedule Meeting is author-constructed from a template; answer is the exact interval intersection (also stated), so ground truth is exact but the test is as templated as the tool.

evidence.quote: the evaluation and validation of the tools created by the tool maker in a real-world
evidence.support_explanation: Authors state tool evaluation/validation in real-world settings is unresolved (sentence continues "setting is a challenge that needs to be addressed").

evidence.quote: assert ans == the provided answer
evidence.support_explanation: Verification uses the labelled ground-truth answers of the validation samples (oracle signal); in the stream setting labels come from a strong model or a human (see E047).

evidence.quote: for num in range(max_limit + 1):
evidence.support_explanation: Wrapped CRT tool is a bounded linear scan; max_limit comes from the question text ("no more than 1188877 durians"). The exact divisibility condition on the next line is cut off in the published text (see materials note).

evidence.quote: for order in permutations(objects):
evidence.support_explanation: Wrapped LD tool enumerates all 5! orderings; the tool user must translate prose constraints into lambda predicates.

evidence.locator: Appendix D LD tool use case
evidence.quote: lambda order: order.index("green") == len(order) - 2,
evidence.support_explanation: The user-side NL->lambda translation is non-trivial code generation by the lightweight model, so "use" is not a pure argument-extraction step.

evidence.quote: reply unknown if no function can
evidence.support_explanation: Dispatcher outputs a task id or "unknown" given function API descriptions; "unknown" is the cache-miss signal.

Not reported: which of the (up to 5) tool-making trials produced the tool used for Table 2, and how it was selected; the tool-making success rates (Table 3) imply trial-level variation that does not appear in Table 2.

Not reported: the stream procedure (instances cached until enough amassed, then a tool is made) is described but not run; no end-to-end stream accuracy/cost; no evaluation of tool-making from cached instances or of tool refinement.

Not reported: a per-instance program-aided baseline (PAL/PoT) for GPT-3.5 or GPT-4, or a hand-written-tool control; so the gain cannot be split into "code execution" vs "tool made once and reused by a cheaper user".
Not reported: ablation of the verification step, of the dispatcher, or of the 3-demo/3-validation sizes; verification is said to repair 2/60 (E010) and mostly supplies demonstrations (E004).

Not reported: confidence intervals, seeds or across-tool-making-run variance for the headline accuracies (tool-making T=0.3 is stochastic; tool use T=0.0). 240 test items per task gives a roughly +/-3 pt binomial band that is not stated.
Not reported: measured token/dollar totals, tool-prompt length vs CoT prompt length, cost of failed tool-making trials and retries, dispatcher cost ("marginal" is asserted), or break-even n.

evidence.quote: Search/Extended Euclidean Interval intersections
evidence.support_explanation: Table 1 lists the generated functions per task (images for most cells); the CRT cell mentions Extended Euclidean while the appendix tool shown is a bounded scan.

evidence.quote: return sorted(word_list)
evidence.support_explanation: Word Sorting tool is one stdlib call; tasks are programmatically trivial/templated, bounding scope of "complex reasoning" claims.

evidence.quote: Wang et al. (2023) conducted research within the Minecraft environment and demonstrated the ability of an LLM-powered agent to acquire new skills in the form of programs.
evidence.support_explanation: Voyager as concurrent skill-library neighbor, described only in one sentence.

evidence.quote: proposes a method of decomposing problem-solving for each individual instance into an abstract tool creation phase
evidence.support_explanation: CREATOR as concurrent neighbor (per-instance abstract tool creation), described only in one sentence.

evidence.quote: either solving it with a powerful model or, if necessary, invoking a human labeler.
evidence.support_explanation: Cache-miss handling in the stream setting: labels/solutions come from a strong model or a human, not from verified execution; this path is not evaluated.

signatures.object: Task-class-specific tool: a Python function plus NL-question->function-call use-case demos, stored as a non-weight artifact; baseline = no tool (few-shot CoT / direct few-shot prompting)
signatures.information: Tool maker (GPT-4 mainly; GPT-3.5 in ablation) sees 3 labelled demonstrations and 3 labelled validation samples, plus execution errors and assertion failures; does not see the 240 test instances
signatures.operation: Propose function by programming-by-example; on execution error append message and retry (<=3); LLM writes unit tests (parse question -> call -> assert ans == provided answer) on validation samples and runs them; on test failure fix only the test call parsing; wrap passing function with the use-case demos
signatures.output: Wrapped tool text (function + use cases) per task class; failed trials discarded
signatures.conditions: Retry threshold 3; T=0.3 in tool making; 8192-context GPT-4 preferred because the whole history is kept (Sec 5.5)
signatures.feedback: Interpreter errors (executability) and unit-test assertions against ground-truth labels (3 samples)
signatures.selection_rule: Admit if the function executes and passes the 3 asserted validation tests within the retry budget; otherwise the trial counts as failed. Selection among the 5 reported trials for downstream use is not specified (E037)
signatures.persistence: Wrapped tool kept as the tool-user prompt and as an API entry in the dispatcher repository; no versioning, rollback, expiry or refinement (E024)
signatures.later_use: All later instances of the same task class: tool user prompt (E006); dispatcher routing (E007)
signatures.claimed_effect: GPT-3.5 + GPT-4-made tool reaches 79.7-100% on six task classes, matching GPT-4 on most (E001,E011,E012)
signatures.failure_boundary: GPT-3.5 as maker fails 0/5 on LD, TSO, Schedule; GPT-4 maker 3/5 on LD and Schedule; tools can overfit to training samples (E016,E017,E018); verification repairs only 2/60 (E010)

signatures.object: Per-instance behaviour of a lightweight tool-user LLM, conditioned in context on the wrapped tool
signatures.information: Wrapped tool (function + demos) and the test question; no weights change; single API call at T=0
signatures.operation: Translate the NL question into function-call arguments (for Logical Deduction, into lambda constraints), execute the function, optionally post-process to the answer format
signatures.output: Final answer from the Python function output
signatures.conditions: User must retain in-context ability (instruction-tuned older GPT-3 models underperform; Table 4); GPT-4 as user can over-solve arguments on Dyck (E015)
signatures.selection_rule: not_applicable (no candidate selection at use time)
signatures.later_use: Each of 240 test instances per task
signatures.claimed_effect: Large gains over few-shot CoT at GPT-3.5 level (e.g. CRT 0.0 -> 100.0, Schedule 18.9 -> 100.0, Dyck 20.4 -> 92.2) at about GPT-3.5 per-call cost
signatures.failure_boundary: LD 79.7 vs GPT-4 CoT 88.8; user model capability and prompt length effects not costed (E042)

signatures.object: Dispatcher LLM + functional tool cache (routing and cache-miss handling)
signatures.information: API descriptions of existing tools and the incoming question; outputs a task name or "unknown"
signatures.operation: Look up a matching tool else mark as novel; novel instances are solved by a strong model or a human labeler and cached until enough are amassed to craft a new tool (design, Sec 4)
signatures.output: Routing decision (use tool X / request tool making)
signatures.conditions: GPT-3.5 as dispatcher; test sets of 100 mixed samples
signatures.feedback: none beyond classification correctness in evaluation
signatures.selection_rule: LLM prompt decision (E036); no threshold or conflict policy described
signatures.persistence: Repository of tool APIs (E007); growth by new tools in design only
signatures.later_use: Each incoming instance in a stream
signatures.claimed_effect: 95% +/- 2% correct tool identification; 96% +/- 3% correct tool-making request on cache misses (E019); "maintaining high performance" in streams (E020)
signatures.failure_boundary: End-to-end stream accuracy/cost, tool creation from cached instances and refinement are not run (E038,E047)

gap.author_gap: Tool-using methods depend on pre-existing tools (E028); serving all instances with a strong LLM is costly while lightweight models fail complex tasks (E029).
gap.checked_gap: Checked against the text: the weak-model failure is real and large on algorithmic tasks under CoT/direct prompting (CRT 0.0, Schedule 18.9, Dyck 20.4 for GPT-3.5; E012) and a GPT-4/GPT-3.5 price ratio >15x is stated (E013). "Tools must exist" is background; the specific fixed non-weight object being changed is the tool inventory / task-class function, produced by the model instead of supplied by humans. The comparison that would show the residual over per-instance code (PAL/PoT) is not made (E039).
lineage: CoT / few-shot prompting (Wei et al.; Suzgun et al. for BigBench demos)
Program-aided reasoning: PAL, Program of Thoughts, Chameleon (per-instance code execution; E027)
Tool-use LLMs: ReAct, Toolformer, TALM, HuggingGPT, ART (tools pre-supplied)
Self-debug / self-refine (execution-error repair; cited in Sec 3.1)
Concurrent tool/skill creation: CREATOR (per-instance abstract/concrete tool creation; E046), Voyager (program skills in Minecraft; E045)
Cost-aware serving: FrugalGPT / LLM cascades, speculative decoding, GPTCache response caching (Sec 1-2)
gap.closest_adjacent: CREATOR (tool creation by decomposing each instance into abstract creation and concrete application) and Voyager (verified program skills reused across tasks) make and reuse code artifacts concurrently; PAL/PoT use code per instance. LATM adds: one tool per task class from a few demos, strong-maker/weak-user cost split, dispatcher functional cache. Per the authors' own text only; neighbour full texts are not in the pinned input pack.
gap.residue: Whether a lightweight model could get the same gain by writing its own per-instance code; whether tools survive realistic, non-templated and drifting tasks; how tool quality is assured and tools are updated after deployment (E024,E031).
gap.stakes: If valid, per-task-class tools let a cheap model replace repeated strong-model calls (analytic O(nc + C) saving at C>15c, E013); if the tools are narrow or mis-verified, errors replicate across all reuses (E018).
gap.method_response: Strong model writes and test-validates a reusable function once; cheap model maps questions to calls; a dispatcher routes and triggers new tool making.
gap.remaining_gap: Tool refinement/upgrade (E024); real-world tool validation (E031); stream end-to-end evaluation (E038); per-instance code and hand-written-tool baselines (E039); measured cost (E042).
unresolved: Closest-neighbour source texts (CREATOR 2305.14318, PAL, PoT, EVAPORATE/Arora et al., FrugalGPT, GPTCache) are not pinned in this input pack; their distinction from LATM rests on LATM's own related-work text. Voyager is a concurrent neighbour and was not read in the pinned input.
Current relevance of later tool-making/skill-library work is not assessed.

rs_pattern.reason: LATM operationally splits one task into maker-side artifact creation and user-side NL->call interfacing, with a Python interpreter as the sound solver and unit tests as the checker. Read in full: decompose_and_delegate (+C25) and adapt_via_conditioning (+C03). adapt_via_conditioning is not chosen: the wrapped tool is in-context conditioning, but there is no canonical schema across a task family, no held-out-category generalisation and no upstream tuning, so it would be a mention not an execution. reframe_as_solvable_object (overview only) is not chosen: no new mathematical object or equivalence is introduced.

revision_proposals: PROPOSAL ONLY (unchecked): add a H07 sub-condition on "maker/user model split with amortisation accounting", requiring failed tool-making trials, retries, dispatcher and prompt-length cost in the cost model; single source (this paper), so not a candidate_pattern.

PROPOSAL ONLY: note in H07 that tool creation may be triggered by task-class from a few labelled demos rather than a live capability gap, and that verification may serve as demonstration extraction rather than repair; single source.
Per A5: the crystallize main card lesson "Let a strong model build tools once and a cheaper one invoke them" was not used as evidence or anchor for this paper.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: C25: learned model emits an executable artifact and a sound solver returns verifiable output ; H07: forge executable tool, check by execution against known answers, register and reuse. In LATM the tool-maker artifact (function + asserted call) is the C25 handoff object and also the H07 registered tool; the tool-user call is the per-instance concretisation.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_and_differences: Shared: execution as the checker, artifact registered for reuse. Differences: C25 centres on solver feedback closing the loop during construction (weak in LATM: repairs 2/60) and on per-instance delegation; H07 centres on a live capability gap, traceback repair and retained-inventory ablation; LATM triggers tool making per task class from 3 demos and does not ablate the retained inventory. Mapping is operation-level, not a name match.

claims.text: LATM with GPT-4 maker + GPT-3.5 user matches GPT-4 as both maker and user on six task classes (Abstract; Sec 5.3)
claims.setting: 6 tasks: LD(5), TSO(5), Dyck, Word Sorting, CRT, Schedule Meeting; tool by GPT-4; users GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4; single tool-using API call T=0
claims.baseline_control: few-shot CoT (first four tasks), direct few-shot prompting (CRT, Schedule); GPT-4 LATM
claims.selection_vs_test: tool from 3 train + 3 validation; test = 240 disjoint instances per task; trial selection unspecified
claims.allowed_conclusion: On these six templated algorithmic task classes the reused GPT-4-made function lets GPT-3.5 reach 79.7-100% on 240 held-out items, within about 1-9 points of GPT-4 (Logical Deduction is the 9-point shortfall vs GPT-4 CoT) and well above its own CoT; "equivalent" is true for 5 of 6 tasks, author-reported, uncertainty not reported.

claims.text: Significantly reduced inference cost via amortised tool making (Abstract; Table 2 cost column)
claims.setting: Analytic cost model O(nc + C), C>15c
claims.result_denominator: no measured totals; Table 4 per-token prices only
claims.allowed_conclusion: Under the stated cost model and price ratio the per-instance cost approaches GPT-3.5 for large n; measured savings, failed-trial cost and break-even n are not shown.

claims.text: A strong model is needed for tool making; tool-user capability trade-off (Sec 5.5)
claims.setting: 5 trials per maker/task; six user models with the same tool
claims.baseline_control: GPT-3.5 maker vs GPT-4 maker; ada..davinci users
claims.selection_vs_test: n/5 success counts; Table 4 on test sets
claims.result_denominator: GPT-3.5 0/5 on LD, TSO, Schedule; GPT-4 3/5, 4/5, 3/5
claims.allowed_conclusion: In these runs a GPT-3.5 maker fails on the three harder tasks and GPT-4 succeeds in 60-100% of trials; small counts.

claims.text: Reusing CoT from a larger model does not help; code tools do (Sec 5.5, Table 5)
claims.setting: 2 tasks (LD, TSO); GPT-4 zero-shot CoT as artifact for GPT-3.5
claims.allowed_conclusion: For these two tasks, code beats both CoT variants; says nothing about per-instance program-aided prompting.

claims.text: A dispatcher enables a functional cache and on-the-fly tool creation in a task stream (Sec 4, 5.4)
claims.selection_vs_test: dispatcher test sets distinct from tool-making data (not stated in detail)
claims.allowed_conclusion: A prompted LLM can route among six known tool APIs and flag unseen tasks with about 95% accuracy; streaming end-to-end performance and cache growth are not shown.

claims.text: Closed-loop framework where LLMs create their own reusable tools (retained, improving)
claims.setting: tool made once per task class; no refinement
claims.allowed_conclusion: Tool creation and reuse are shown for a fixed task class; no loop in which later feedback improves tools or the maker (no improver-level evidence).

assessment.evidence_level_note: A non-weight artifact (verified Python tool + demos) built from 3+3 instances is reused on 240 disjoint test instances per task with large gains over no-tool baselines (E008,E012); this satisfies retained for the single-round reuse claim. Not improver: the maker/tool is never revised from later feedback (E024). Scope: same task classes, templated, author-reported only; no per-instance-code control (E039), so the gain is not attributable to tool making and reuse as opposed to code execution alone.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: On six templated algorithmic task classes, a GPT-4-written and 3-sample-tested Python function plus three NL->call demos lets GPT-3.5 Turbo reach 79.7-100% accuracy on 240 held-out items per task, near GPT-4 on 5 of 6 tasks and far above its own CoT/direct baselines (author-reported); cost advantage follows an analytic model with C>15c; maker/user capacity effects and the CoT-artifact control are reported.

G.reason: Specific, source-backed bottleneck: tools must pre-exist (E028) and serving everything with a strong model is costly (E029), with a concrete diagnostic that weak models fail algorithmic tasks under CoT (CRT 0.0, Schedule 18.9, Dyck 20.4; E012). Nearest neighbours named (PAL/PoT/Chameleon E027; Voyager E045; CREATOR E046) with stated differentiators (reuse + maker/user cost split, E026), remaining gap partly stated (refine/upgrade tools E024; real-world validation E031). Held at 3: neighbours are only characterised in 1-2 sentences, no empirical comparison, the key rival (per-instance PAL with the same models) is not engaged (E039), and neighbour texts are not pinned locally.

M.reason: Operation chain is reconstructable: 3 labelled demos -> PbE function, error-driven retries (E002), unit tests on 3 validation samples with ground-truth asserts (E003,E032), wrapping into function+use-case demos (E006), reuse by a cheaper user and routing by a dispatcher (E007,E036). Mechanism is causally argued (exact computation goes to the interpreter, the weak model only maps NL to a call; E034,E035) and yields distinguishing predictions that were tested: weak maker fails (E016,E017), reusing CoT text instead of code does not help (E022,E023). Held at 3, not 4: the verification/admission assumption is thin (repairs only 2/60, never repairs the function; E003,E010; demos/validation of size 3 allow non-general tools, E018), and the stream/cache path that carries the "closed-loop" and "functional cache" claims is a described design whose tool-creation step is not specified or tested (E038,E047).

X.reason: Main steps, prompts (App C), wrapped tools (App D) and settings (k=3 demos, 3 validation samples, retry 3, T=0.3/0.0; E002,E003,E009) are given, and the next-round read is explicit (tool user prompt = wrapped tool; E006). But the execution conditions that SCORE_SPEC weights most are thin: the retention gate is 3 asserted samples (E003,E032) and only the test calls, not the function, are repaired on failure; no versioning, rollback, expiry or conflict handling, and tool refinement is future work (E024); which trial's tool enters Table 2 is unspecified (E037); the stream cache-miss path (amass instances then craft tool) is not specified in executable detail or run (E038,E047). Implementation detail not_reported: the CRT divisibility condition and the date-format strings in the Appendix D code are cut off in the published text (coordinator verified the same loss in both the v2 PDF and HTML renderings; the PDF text was checked here); treated as an author-side clarity defect that does not block the core judgement because function structure, inputs and outputs remain visible (E033). Code URL gives no credit.
search_scope: Appendix D CRT and Schedule Meeting tool code lines: v2 PDF text read; coordinator reports same loss in v2 HTML

E.measurement.reason: Metric is accuracy on 240 disjoint test instances per task against exact ground truth (BigBench answers; Schedule Meeting answer computed exactly from interval intersection; E008,E030), tool use at T=0 with a single API call (Sec 5.1). The verifier cannot be gamed because answers are deterministic. Not 4: no trivial-baseline check (e.g. 20% chance on five-option tasks), no error breakdown beyond Dyck (E015), dispatcher is scored only as classification (E019), and tool correctness beyond the benchmark is explicitly open (E031). Cost measurement is judged in E.cost, baseline strength in E.causality.

E.causality.reason: Relevant controls exist: CoT/direct few-shot (E012,E014), tool-maker and tool-user capacity sweeps (E016,E017,E021), and a CoT-as-retained-artifact control on two tasks that does not match code (E022,E023). Key controls missing: no per-instance PAL/PoT baseline with GPT-3.5/GPT-4, so gain from code execution cannot be separated from tool making and reuse (E039); no verification, dispatcher or demo-count ablation, with the authors' own 2/60 repair figure suggesting verification is not what carries results (E040,E010); no hand-written-tool control; baselines are weaker on CRT/Schedule (direct prompting, no CoT; E014); "closed-loop" improvement and cumulative tool growth are not tested (E038). Maker/user division itself is supported by the two sweeps.

E.holdout.reason: Tool is built from 3+3 instances and scored on 240 disjoint instances per task (E008), so selection and test are separated for the reuse claim; dispatcher is tested on separate sampled sets (E019). Deductions: ground-truth answers are an oracle signal inside tool making (E032) and in the stream setting labels would come from a strong model or human (E047); which trial's tool was reported is unspecified, so selection leakage cannot be excluded (E037); no contamination discussion for public BigBench tasks with GPT-4; six templated algorithmic task classes with test drawn from the same generator (E030,E044), no new-task transfer; the stream-claim scope is not covered end-to-end (E020,E038).

E.statistics.reason: Per A2 ladder: tool-making trials are repeated (5 per model-task) with success counts including failures (E017), dispatcher accuracy is reported with spread over repeated test-set constructions (E019), and test size is stated (E008). But headline Table 2 accuracies carry no interval, seed or across-trial variance (tool-making is stochastic at T=0.3; E041) and the 5-trial counts are tiny.

E.cost.reason: Cost is central to the claim and is modelled explicitly as O(nc + C) with C>15c, so amortisation is acknowledged (E013), and Table 4 lists per-token prices for tool-user models (E021). But no measured token/dollar totals, no prompt-length comparison (wrapped tool + demos vs CoT), failed tool-making trials (up to 40-100% failure for some maker/task pairs; E017) and retries are not counted, dispatcher cost is only asserted as marginal, no break-even n and no equal-budget comparison (E042).
